title: Wood – the Multisensory, Physiological Magician
author: RN Collins
standfirst: “Current evidence on the effect of wood spans sensory, physiological, and environmental dimensions. We know there are many measurable neurophysiological responses. Direct experimental studies remain limited in some areas, particularly long-term exposure and optimal wood proportions, but the existing research provides a great deal of guidance to help biophilic design practice.”

sections.x: Wood as multisensory signal

Wood directly influences how our nervous systems interpret safety, calm, and environmental coherence (Burnard & Kutnar, 2015). The autonomic nervous system has two branches: sympathetic (activating stress responses) and parasympathetic (supporting rest and recovery). Exposure to wood consistently shifts this balance toward parasympathetic dominance.
Visual Processing

Looking at wood surfaces reduces sympathetic activation and increases parasympathetic activity. Laboratory studies document lower blood pressure, reduced heart rate, and improved mood in wood interiors versus synthetic materials (Tsunetsugu et al., 2007; Fell, 2010).

Why? The mechanism appears linked to visual processing efficiency. Irregular, fractal-like patterns in wood grain align with stimuli our brains evolved to process with minimal cognitive effort. Visual stress decreases and attentional resources stay preserved.
Tactile and Thermal Properties

Lower thermal conductivity creates warmth that metal, concrete, and plastic can’t match (Nyrud & Bringslimark, 2010). The brain processes warm, natural materials as less threatening. Baseline arousal lowers.
A cold metal handrail versus a wooden one: the sensory discomfort from cold metal requires cognitive resources to manage. Across thousands of daily interactions, this adds up.
Olfactory Contributions

Certain wood species emit volatile organic compounds (VOCs), particularly phytoncides like alpha-pinene. At low concentrations, these reduce stress markers and enhance immune function (Tsunetsugu et al., 2010). Indoor wood doesn’t replicate forest-bathing concentrations, but even subtle olfactory cues influence mood and perceived comfort.
Acoustic Properties

Sound absorption and diffusion reduce reverberation and auditory stress (Asdrubali et al., 2017). Excessive reverberation forces continuous filtering of irrelevant stimuli – what researchers call cognitive load, the mental effort required to process information and maintain attention.
Wood-moderated acoustics create environments that feel calmer and more intelligible (Shield & Dockrell, 2003). Focus and emotional stability improve.
Integrated Effect
Multiple sensory channels communicate safety simultaneously.
Wood, stress, and attention

How the nervous system continuously interprets environments as safe or threatening determines stress regulation and attention. Materials shape this interpretation. Chronic sympathetic activation correlates with anxiety, impaired emotional regulation, and cognitive fatigue (McEwen & Akil, 2020).
Wood appears to shift occupants out of stress-reactive states without creating under-stimulation.
Preserving Cognitive Bandwidth
Spaces that are high-noise, visually chaotic, or acoustically harsh force continuous filtering. This depletes cognitive resources needed for work, learning, or decision-making.
Through acoustic and visual properties, wood moderates these demands. Speech intelligibility improves. “Soft fascination” allows attention to settle instead of scattering (Zhang et al., 2023).
Long-Term Effects

Environments that subtly lower stress and cognitive load influence baseline arousal levels when exposure is repeated. Long-term emotional regulation improves. Attentional resilience strengthens. This is particularly relevant where people spend extended periods – offices, schools, healthcare facilities, civic institutions.
Wood supports mental performance not through stimulation but through reduced effort. It quietly shapes physiological state, attentional capacity, and emotional balance.
Applications across building types

Clinical anxiety in hospitals. Cognitive demands in classrooms. Psychological weight in courthouses. Some environments carry inherent stress. Material choices either compound these challenges or support recovery and regulation.
Healthcare Settings

Hospital interiors with wood finishes show consistent patterns: lower patient blood pressure, reduced heart rate, improved mood. These physiological shifts matter clinically. Stress impairs immune function, slows healing, and increases pain perception (Ulrich et al., 1991).

Clinician burnout and emotional exhaustion worsen in high-noise, visually sterile environments (Ulrich et al., 2008). Acoustic absorption and visual warmth from wood moderate environmental stressors. Concentration and emotional regulation during long shifts receive support. Healthcare environments with wood support both healing and caregiving.
Educational Environments

Learning outcomes suffer in classrooms with excessive noise, glare, and visual monotony. Children with attentional or sensory sensitivities face particular challenges. Natural materials correlate with improved concentration, reduced stress, and more positive classroom behavior. Both academic performance and emotional development benefit.

Warm, tactile materials signal safety and predictability to developing nervous systems in early childhood and special education settings. This likely matters for learning and emotional growth. For students navigating trauma or neurodivergence, environments that reduce sensory stress can meaningfully influence engagement and retention.
Institutional and Civic Spaces

Courthouses, administrative buildings, and civic institutions often carry associations with authority, judgment, bureaucratic complexity. The brain processes cold or harsh materials as heightening anxiety and defensiveness. Natural materials promote calm appraisal and support the clarity of thought and constructive interaction these spaces should facilitate.

Libraries exemplify this. Acoustically balanced, visually warm environments support sustained attention and reduce mental fatigue during prolonged cognitive tasks. Sound absorption and visual softening from wood make it particularly suited for spaces intended for focus, reflection, and information processing.
Wood and carbon storage

About 40% of global carbon emissions come from the built environment, making material selection a central climate mitigation lever (IPCC, 2022). Wood occupies a unique position: structural material, carbon store, and – when responsibly sourced – renewable resource.
Embodied Carbon

Life-cycle assessments demonstrate that timber construction carries lower embodied carbon than steel or concrete alternatives. Carbon sequestration during growth and reduced processing energy drive this advantage (Peñaloza et al., 2019; Amiri et al., 2020).
Wood holds atmospheric carbon for decades when incorporated into buildings while displacing carbon-intensive materials.
Forest Management Determines Outcomes

Climate benefits from wood depend entirely on forest management and supply-chain transparency. Sustainably managed forests maintain ecosystem services: soil stability, water regulation, habitat provision (Pan et al., 2011). Poorly managed extraction negates climate gains through biodiversity loss and carbon leakage.
Designers and developers must verify sourcing. Certification systems like FSC provide verification frameworks (FSC, 2021). The question: which wood, from where, harvested how.
Circular Systems

Compatibility with reuse, disassembly, and biodegradation at end-of-life means wood supports circular systems (Gagnon et al., 2019). Buildings with exposed or modular wood elements facilitate adaptive reuse, extending lifespans and reducing demolition resource intensity.

Hybrid systems combining structural performance with ecological function also become possible. Mass timber structures can integrate green roofs, vegetated façades, and passive climate strategies, creating buildings that moderate temperature, support biodiversity, and reduce operational energy demand.
Psychological Connection

Visible wood use reinforces psychological connections between occupants and ecological processes. Awareness of material origin and ecological impact influences occupant satisfaction, perceived environmental responsibility, and pro-environmental behavior (Kellert, 2018). Buildings that express material cycles through exposed timber, reuse narratives, or landscape integration strengthen occupants’ sense of ecological participation.
Addressing common concerns
Misconceptions about wood persist.
Fire Safety

Modern mass timber systems – cross-laminated timber (CLT) and glue-laminated timber (glulam) – perform predictably in fire through char formation, which insulates structural cores and slows combustion. Fire testing demonstrates that properly designed assemblies meet or exceed fire-resistance ratings required for steel or concrete when combined with appropriate detailing (Gagnon et al., 2019; IPCC, 2022).
Mass timber performs very differently than light-frame construction. Conflating the two generates misplaced concern.
Durability

Moisture management, not material choice, determines building longevity. Appropriate detailing, ventilation, and maintenance allow wood’s service life to equal or exceed conventional materials (Amiri et al., 2020).
Most failures attributed to wood stem from design or construction errors: inadequate drainage, poor enclosure performance, insufficient ventilation. These are predictable, preventable issues.
Indoor Air Quality

VOC emissions from wood products occur, particularly when treated with adhesives, finishes, or preservatives. Untreated or low-emission products typically have low emissions that material selection and ventilation strategies can manage (Nyrud & Bringslimark, 2010).
Improved perceived air quality and occupant comfort have been associated with exposure to natural wood surfaces. Sensory benefits can coexist with healthy IAQ when products are responsibly specified.
Equity and Access

High-profile, high-cost developments often feature biophilic and mass-timber projects, raising legitimate access concerns. Without intentional policy and procurement strategies, wood-centred design risks remaining an amenity for the privileged (Anguelovski et al., 2022).
Public investment in affordable housing, community-led projects, and institutional buildings is critical for equitable benefit distribution (Hoffman et al., 2020).
Future Research Needs

Binary comparisons (wood vs. no wood) dominate most studies rather than optimal proportions or distributions. Tsunetsugu et al.’s (2007) finding that 45% wood coverage produced different physiological responses than 90% coverage suggests non-linear relationships.

Questions remain: What wood proportions optimize different outcomes? How do placement patterns (ceiling vs. walls vs. floors) differentially affect occupants? Do effects vary by species, grain patterns, or finish treatments?
Long-Term Exposure

Exposure periods of 90 seconds to 2 hours characterize most experimental studies. Whether benefits persist, strengthen, or attenuate with continuous long-term exposure remains unclear. Longitudinal studies tracking occupant responses over months or years would clarify cumulative effects.
Population Variability

Young adults predominate in current studies. How age, cultural background, neurodivergence, trauma history, or sensory processing differences modulate responses requires investigation. Special populations – children, elderly adults, individuals with sensory sensitivities – may experience different effect sizes or require different design strategies.
Mechanism Clarification

Sympathetic/parasympathetic shifts are well-documented, but precise neural pathways remain incompletely mapped. Advanced neuroimaging studies could clarify which brain regions mediate wood’s effects and whether responses involve evolutionary predispositions, learned associations, or both.
Interaction Effects

Wood rarely appears in isolation. How it interacts with other biophilic elements (natural light, views, plants, water features) requires systematic investigation. Do effects combine additively or synergistically? Do diminishing returns emerge?
Economic Analysis

Limited cost-benefit analyses comparing wood vs. conventional materials across full lifecycles exist. Documentation of implementation barriers, successful procurement strategies, and equity-promoting policies would support wider adoption. Case studies tracking health outcomes, productivity metrics, and energy performance in wood buildings would strengthen the business case.
Climate and Cultural Context

Most research originates from Japan, Northern Europe, and North America. Whether findings generalize across climates, architectural traditions, and cultural contexts requires investigation. Regional wood species, traditional building practices, and cultural associations with wood may modulate effects.
Conclusion

Human health, ecological responsibility, and design ethics converge around wood. When responsibly sourced and applied with scientific understanding, wood-based materials can simultaneously support stress regulation, cognitive restoration, and climate mitigation.

The evidence base is substantial. Wood moderates sensory load, improves affective states, and supports parasympathetic activation across healthcare, education, and institutional environments, particularly in high-stress contexts. At planetary scale, life-cycle assessments demonstrate that mass timber and engineered wood products substantially reduce embodied carbon compared to steel and concrete, especially when forests are managed as long-term carbon sinks.

Yet this potential remains contingent. Rigorous certification, supply-chain accountability, and attention to social equity are necessary. Without these, wood risks becoming another extractive material masked by sustainability rhetoric.

Material science can align with biological reality and climate urgency. Environments that calm instead of overstimulate. Restoration instead of depletion. Regeneration instead of extraction. When integrated thoughtfully through responsible sourcing, appropriate detailing, and context-sensitive application, wood functions as connective tissue between human well-being and planetary health.
